author: Vitor
notes: Got a TLE by attempting to simulate and count all possible `n` rows.
aiExplanation: This solution builds a full **`n × 10` boolean grid** (`matrix`) where `true` marks a reserved seat, filling it from `reservedSeats` (subtracting 1 to convert 1-based rows/seats to 0-based indexes). It then scans every row, checking the three possible 4-seat family windows starting at columns `1`, `3`, and `5` (seats 2–5, 4–7, and 6–9); if all four seats in a window are free, it counts a family (`res++`) and jumps ahead an extra two columns (`col += 2`) so the next check starts past the seats just used, which prevents overlapping families. The answer is the total `res`. The logic is correct, but because it allocates and iterates over **every row** even when `n` is huge and most rows have no reservations, it runs in `O(n)` time and memory and ends up **too slow (TLE)** for large inputs.

author: Vitor
notes: A much better solution: assume maximum seats taken, discount only where there are reserved seats.
aiExplanation: This solution avoids touching every row by only looking at rows that actually have reservations: it builds a **`Map` from row number to a `Set` of reserved seats**, then starts with the optimistic answer `res = n * 2` (every row can seat two families when fully empty). For each reserved row it checks four seat pairs — `start` (seats 2–3), `mid1` (4–5), `mid2` (6–7), and `end` (8–9) — and combines them into the three possible family placements: `free0` (seats 2–5), `free2` (seats 6–9), and `free1` (seats 4–7). If both `free0` and `free2` are available the row still fits two families and nothing changes; otherwise, if at least one of the three placements is free it loses one family (`res--`), and if none fit it loses both (`res -= 2`). Because the work depends only on the number of reserved seats rather than `n`, it runs in `O(reservedSeats.length)` time, which is why it passes where the grid approach timed out.
